nodes.claim: The perfect display is one geometry that every scale shares — you, your city, the world, and every axiom drawn in the same space with the same grammar.
nodes.detail: InSight already runs one telescope (you→world) and one plane (the patterns Map); the perfect version unifies them: a single navigable space where zooming changes cohort, not metaphor, and where each axiom is a region or direction rather than a separate screen. The corner-doors instinct (connections radiating every direction) is this node's UI shadow. To argue: specify the geometry (what is distance, what is direction, what is size) at every zoom without a metaphor switch.

nodes.claim: Distance means exactly one thing per view — and so does every other channel the frame contains; a display that mixes meanings in one frame is wrong regardless of how it tests.
nodes.detail: Raised argued→cited 2026-08-26; adversarially checked the same run. The rule itself is normative — a claim about what a display owes its reader, not a prediction — so the empirical spatialization literature grounds the PREMISE the rule rests on: every channel present in a frame gets read, whether or not the designer assigned it a meaning. (1) Viewers default to straight-line metric distance: across display types there is no significant difference between 'default' and 'direct' distance instructions — people interpret default distance instructions as direct straight-line distance (Fabrikant & Montello 2008, the strongest single result here). The 2004 network-display study is cited for its design, which explicitly separated direct Euclidean distance, cumulative path length, topological hop count and link visual variables as competing 'distances' (Fabrikant et al. 2004); its effect direction is deliberately not asserted — full text was unreachable this run and secondary summaries conflict. (2) The mapping from distance to MEANING is not automatic, and competing visual structure overrides distance when present: the first-law experiments 'largely support' distance-as-similarity while finding non-distance display characteristics also move similarity judgments (Montello et al. 2003); when regions are drawn, region membership largely determines judged similarity, beating metric distance, with hue modifying it further (Fabrikant, Montello & Mark 2006); and the information-landscape metaphor is an outright negative result — the metaphor is not self-evident to lay users (Fabrikant, Montello & Mark 2010). Two consequences this node draws as its OWN design inferences, downstream of that premise: (a) the semantic table this node demands must cover every channel the frame contains, and the perfect display omits channels it has no assigned meaning for; (b) one carve-out, forced by map-4's evidence: a channel may carry its one meaning plus a DECLARED modifier of that meaning's evidential weight — uncertainty-about-X drawn by suppressing X's own channel (the value-suppressing-palette pattern) is one composite semantic, stated in the table, not a second meaning smuggled into the frame. What the rule forbids is unassigned or double-booked meaning, not declared composite meaning. InSight's live shadow: the People lens states its distance out loud ('the model's expected disagreement between two people, beyond each question's popularity' — docs/PEOPLE-MAP.md on main); this node says the rest of any frame owes the same sentence. Verification grade: all five sources verified at abstract level against multiple independent indexes, re-checked by a separate adversarial pass; no within-study numbers are asserted.
sources: Montello DR, Fabrikant SI, Ruocco M, Middleton RS 2003, 'Testing the First Law of Cognitive Geography on Point-Display Spatializations', COSIT 2003, LNCS 2825:316-331, DOI 10.1007/978-3-540-39923-0_21

nodes.claim: Authored anchors and learned embedding combine in ONE persistent space: stability must be structural — the space itself persists and updates incrementally — never post-hoc alignment, and it is a measured trade-off, not a free win.
nodes.detail: Raised conjecture→cited 2026-08-26; adversarially checked the same run. The claim is refined by the evidence in three ways. First, the seed's premise ('a re-fit teleports everything and destroys spatial memory') traces to Misue et al. 1995, which introduced the mental map and its three formal models (orthogonal ordering, proximity, topology) as an ASSUMPTION, not a finding — the paper is conceptual/algorithmic — and twenty years of experiments then made the picture conditional: stability demonstrably helps orientation and route-finding in an evolving layout — significantly faster, fewer errors, holding as the number of targets increases (Archambault & Purchase, GD 2012) — which is precisely the Map's task class (a space the user learns, leaves, and re-enters), while for general dynamic-graph comprehension 'no experiment has found conclusive evidence that supports the effectiveness of the mental map' (Archambault & Purchase 2013, their own summary), early tests confirmed the assumption only for some task categories (Purchase, Hoggan & Görg 2007), and one study found simple mental-map preservation no better than optimizing static aesthetics per frame (Saffrey & Purchase 2008). Second, the effect is non-monotonic: graph sequences with HIGH or LOW mental-map preservation both beat MEDIUM preservation (Purchase & Samra 2008, 'Extremes Are Better'; the authors themselves read the U-shape partly as individual preference). Read by analogy — that study varied an algorithmic preservation parameter, not anchoring — this node treats half-pinning as the medium case and argues anchoring must be structural, not cosmetic; the transfer is this node's own inference, recorded as such. Third, on mechanism the projection literature agrees and prices it: dynamic t-SNE adds an explicit movement penalty λ, an explicitly controllable trade-off between temporal coherence and per-step projection reliability in which strong pinning costs fidelity (Rauber et al. 2016); that trade-off has since been formally defined and measured — Vernier et al. 2020 contribute spatial and temporal stability metrics plus benchmarks for exactly this property — and guided variants steer points with global anchors (Vernier et al. 2021, PCD-tSNE/LD-tSNE: learned positions pinned to stable guides, peer-reviewed). Two results push the mechanism one step past the seed. Re-fit-then-align — the orthogonal-Procrustes recipe used at scale by Hamilton et al. 2016 — is itself a documented noise source in diachronic word embeddings, transferred here by analogy: Dubossarsky et al. 2019 show alignment noise corrupts downstream measurement and a formulation that never fits separate spaces outperforms alignment models on synthetic and manual test sets. And a learned parametric map supports fast online embedding of new data (Sainburg, McInnes & Gentner 2021) — that new points can land without moving old ones, because nothing re-fits, is this node's inference from that mechanism. So the perfect layout is not 'learned, then pinned back'; it is one persistent space, incrementally updated, whose per-update movement is a published, budgeted quantity — the display-side analogue of pat-2's auditability, which is what the depends edge now means. Tooling note recorded so no later run cites it wrongly: AlignedUMAP, the obvious off-the-shelf tool, has NO method paper by its author's own statement (umap-learn GitHub discussion #966, read at full text this run and re-read by the adversarial pass) — software-docs grade; the peer-reviewed neighbors are 2-MAP (Liu et al., WACV 2020) and the Rauber/Vernier line. Verification grade: abstract-level for all sources except the two GitHub items (full text); numeric effect sizes were not recoverable this run and none are asserted.

nodes.claim: Uncertainty is geometry, not a footnote: the perfect display makes thin data LOOK thin — outcome uncertainty, encoded frequency-framed in the mark itself.
nodes.detail: Raised argued→cited 2026-08-26 in a narrowed form; adversarially checked the same run (the check corrected four framing errors here before landing — see LOG). Two separable findings, and keeping them separate is the narrowing. HOW to draw uncertainty (encoding form): (1) the default encoding actively misleads — a bar depicting a mean induces within-the-bar bias, points inside the bar judged more likely than points equidistant from the mean outside it (Newman & Scholl 2012), and viewers misinterpret bar+error-bar displays at even basic levels while gradient and violin encodings leave judgments better informed by the margin of error (Correll & Gleicher 2014); (2) making the mark itself carry the evidence changes decisions — value-suppressing uncertainty palettes allocate less of the color channel to values as uncertainty grows, thin data literally drawn less distinguishable, and a crowdsourced evaluation found they push people to weight uncertainty more heavily in decisions (Correll, Moritz & Heer 2018); in an incentivized transit task, 50-quantile dotplots were the best-performing display: +4.4 percentage points of optimal payoff attained versus the no-uncertainty control on the final trial (95% credible interval 2.1–8.3 pp), with 3.9 pp lower performance SD (CI 2.4–5.7 pp), from the authors' Bayesian beta regression — while the advantage over CDFs was not reliably distinguished (1.3 pp, CI −0.1 to 3.2) (Fernandes et al. 2018, the one study this run verified at full text from the authors' published analysis); (3) the frequency/discrete-draw framing beats static density summaries — hypothetical outcome plots outperform error bars and violins for inferences about ordering across two and three quantities, with the advantage concentrated in those multi-quantity questions (Hullman, Resnick & Adar 2015); animated HOPs beat conventional static uncertainty displays for trend judgment (Kale et al. 2019); count-based quantile dotplots beat densities for everyday probabilistic estimates on small screens (Kay et al. 2016). These encoding-form results were largely demonstrated on inferential-uncertainty displays (margins of error) and transfer across uncertainty types as findings about form. WHICH uncertainty to draw is orthogonal, and is where the seed over-claimed: drawing INFERENTIAL uncertainty correctly can inflate perceived effects — 95% confidence intervals made people overestimate and overpay for treatment effects relative to prediction intervals (Hofman et al. 2020) — so the perfect display's 'thin' is outcome/predictive uncertainty: the spread of what actually happens, not the precision of a mean. Recorded so no later run re-inflates the seed: geometry does not beat text per se — in the transit ranking, plain-text quantile intervals outranked the PDF and interval displays on point estimates, though those orderings are not reliably distinguished; ensembles are not automatically honest — summary-cone and spaghetti displays of identical hurricane data produce different interpretations (Padilla, Ruginski & Creem-Regehr 2017, whose ensemble displays also over-weight individual members; Ruginski et al. 2016 for different decisions under different visual properties); a correctly drawn interval can be re-read as deterministic bounds — the deterministic construal error (Savelli & Joslyn's line of work, reviewed in Joslyn & Savelli 2021); one map-decision study found mixed accuracy effects — sometimes improved, sometimes unchanged — alongside strategy shifts (Korporaal et al. 2020); and the field's own methodologists warn the genre is noisy — practiced authors omit uncertainty deliberately, citing credibility costs (Hullman 2020, survey of 90 authors), and only 10 of 39 studies claiming to identify biased behavior gave participants enough information to identify the normative decision (Hullman, Kale & Hartline 2025). The perfect display therefore encodes outcome uncertainty as frequency-framed geometry of the mark itself — draws, dots, suppressed palettes — extending InSight's n=0-draws-nothing refusal continuously; states WHICH uncertainty it drew; and never treats 'uncertainty shown' as 'honesty achieved'. Per map-2's carve-out, a suppressed palette is a declared modifier of a channel's one meaning, stated in the view's semantic table — that is what the supports edge asserts. Verification grade: Fernandes 2018 at full text (authors' analysis file, figures confirmed to the digit by the adversarial pass); all others abstract-level against multiple independent indexes; MacEachren et al. 2012 (Visual Semiotics & Uncertainty Visualization, IEEE TVCG 18(12):2496-2505, DOI 10.1109/TVCG.2012.279) is real and relevant but its performance results could not be verified this run, so its intuitiveness rankings are deliberately not cited.

nodes.claim: Efficiency is a display property: the perfect map is drawable from published aggregates on a phone, with no per-view server work.
nodes.detail: A display theory that needs a server render per interaction is a different (worse) product: slower, costlier, and structurally tempted toward per-user computation. The perfect map reads published, cacheable artifacts (the loadings-doc pattern) and computes layout on device — which also keeps the display layer independently verifiable: anyone can recompute the picture from the same public numbers.
